uncited: It sets itself apart from siblings like [Mip-NeRF 360 MLP Architecture](14098-mip-nerf-360-mlp-architecture.md) by replacing global positional encoding with bone-centric relative metrics, and from [SUDS](14964-suds.md) by relying on explicit skeleton transforms rather than implicit deformation fields.
*   World-space query position $q \in \mathbb{R}^3$.
*   World-space view direction $d \in \mathbb{R}^3$.
*   Skeleton pose parameters $\theta_k$ for frame $k$, defining bone transformations $T(\theta_k, m)$ for each bone $m$.
*   Combined encoding vector $e_k \in \mathbb{R}^D$, which serves as the input to the density/color MLP $F_\phi$.
*   Relative Distance $\tilde{v}_k \in \mathbb{R}^M$: Scalar distance from $q$ to each bone.
*   Relative Direction $\tilde{r}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{3M}$: Unit vector from $q$ to each bone.
*   Relative Ray Direction $\tilde{d}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{3M}$: View direction rotated to local bone frame.
Combine the components into the final input vector $e_k$.
*   **Cutoff Threshold ($t$):** Not given in the sources.
*   **Frequency Bands ($L$):** Not given in the sources (inherited from parent [Model Architecture and Encoding](13550-model-architecture-and-encoding.md)).
The method prefers relative distance for lower dimensionality and better reconstruction accuracy.
*   **Relative Direction Encoding:** The relative direction $\tilde{r}_k$ is passed directly into the final encoding $e_k$ without subsequent positional encoding (PE).
Maps the query $q$ to local coordinates of each bone.
Sets itself apart by preserving full 3D local structure but suffers from high dimensionality.
Computes the L2 norm from $q$ to each bone.
Sets itself apart by being lower-dimensional and capturing radial symmetry of limbs.
Normalizes the bone-relative position vector.
Sets itself apart by providing orientation information without PE.
Rotates the view direction into the local bone frame.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(M \cdot L)$ per query point, where $M$ is the number of bones and $L$ is the number of frequency bands.
The transformation $T^{-1}$ is $O(1)$ per bone.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(M \cdot L)$ for the encoding vector.
The skeleton transforms must be stored or computed on the fly.
*   Incorporates explicit domain knowledge of human articulation.
*   Invariant to global shift and rotation of the person.
*   Preserves piece-wise rigidity of articulated motion.
*   Lower dimensionality compared to full bone-relative position encoding.
*   Requires a skeleton pose estimator for initialization and runtime.
*   Performance depends on the accuracy of the skeleton tracking.
*   Does not model complex soft-tissue deformation (muscle bulging) as explicitly as parametric surface models, though it approximates it via the neural field.
*   **When to use:** Dynamic human avatar rendering where pose information is available or can be estimated.
*   **When not to use:** Static scenes, scenes without articulated structures, or when skeleton tracking is unreliable.
The method was developed to address the limitations of standard NeRF in modeling dynamic humans, where global coordinates fail to capture the rigid motion of body parts.
It inverts the approach of parametric models like SMPL: instead of deforming a surface, it deforms the query space.
The work builds on the foundational NeRF architecture [Model Architecture and Encoding](13550-model-architecture-and-encoding.md) and integrates it with articulated skeleton data.

Skeleton-Relative Encoding transforms 3D query positions and view directions into local bone-relative coordinate systems before processing them through a neural radiance field, explicitly incorporating domain knowledge of human body part linkage [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that Skeleton-Relative Encoding transforms 3D query positions and view directions into local bone-relative coordinate systems before processing them through a neural radiance field, explicitly incorporating domain knowledge of human body part linkage. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 3.3: 'Our core contribution is to transform the query locations q and view direction d relative to the skeleton before determining the color and opacity at that transformed point via NeRF. It is a form of reparameterization that explicitly incorporates domain knowledge of how the human body parts are linked and transformed relative to each other.' The source further details the mathematical transformations for query positions ($q$) and view directions ($d$) into bone-relative coordinates ($ ar{q}$ and $ ar{d}$) and their subsequent use as input to the NeRF network.
